Is all this VR craze just a gyroscopic controller like a Wii U pad just strapped to your face? Or am I missing something here?

You're missing something here. VR is more than a gyroscope with a shitty LCD. It's a complete 3D space position tracking and rendering system that is designed to simulate depth, and take up a large field of view.

So what's different? I watch videos and it looks like playing a Wii U but with the screen and rotation control attached to your head, with the controller broken in half and put in each hand like the Nintendo Nunchucks.

Edit: I see all the downvotes to this comment. But when I responded initially the edit on original commentators post hadn't gone through. The original comment was only "You're missing something here." Then the comment was edited with more info that mirrors the response to my comment.

• no 3d (VR simulates depth)
  • shitty FoV
  • bad framerate
  • no rendering system
  • no API
  • no proper 3d space tracking

You can technically simulate motion and position tracking with only a gyroscope, but it tends to lose synchronization very easily and is not very accurate. I'd suggest trying to find a VR setup somewhere that you can try. It'll take you about 5 seconds to realize that there's simply no comparison.

Not only that, but regardless of naysayers the human brain is hilariously easy to fool. I sat down in a bucket seat to play iRacing in a terribly calibrated Oculus SDK2 - the foam ring was almost completely ripped off, the straps were worn and frayed, and the whole thing was basically towards the end of its lifespan after being abused by the public. Once I managed to adjust to the sweet spot where the image retained some of its clarity and came into focus (due to the low resolution of the prototype, it looked like a blurred newsprint photo), I was able to look around the cockpit of the virtual car that I now sat in.

I mentally checked that the digital arms were easily two inches to the right, thinking that I'd never be immersed due to such a large oversight - but not within even 10 seconds of getting used to the vehicle's manual transmission did I had to check that my subconscious had already accepted these virtual, off-center arms as my own.

"Yes, these arms are mine." is what my brain thought.

They weren't even in the right place, but because they were barely even close enough, the brain of an indie developer and all-around tech lover was duped by something as simple as strapping a screen to his face. Never underestimate VR.

Well, assuming the screens are properly calibrated, you are in the action and with a proper 3D view ( which make things like judging distance much easier )
( and if the screens aren't properly calibrated, you have an headache )

The gyroscopic controller part is just a way to make it more natural to use. ( and most likely to avoid major cases of motion sickness )

Still, those things can be fairly advanced : there's even a prototype which work in a specially constructed warehouse made to trick your sense of space allowing you to move in spaces far larger than the room you're actually in. ( the room still have to be fairly big to prevent you from noticing your straight line is actually making you follow a curve, also they have to track your position within the room itself )

That is exactly what it is, attached to a high dpi screen.

The original wii controller reverse engineered an expensive RC helicopter gyro \ motion \ speed sensor into a single chip. That chip was so much cheaper some RC guys modded it into a self balancing quadcopter controller board, which kicked off the boom in diy quadcopters. Once that chip got added to a phone motherboard the only thing left to do was strap it to your face to get full look-around VR. It's a pretty cool chain of inventions.

The devil is in the "details". A Wii U pad strapped to your face wouldn't work in any reasonable sense of the word "work". You need the lenses, you need the image deformation and color-correction software, you need the very high density, high frequency screen, you need the very accurate motion sensor and positioning system and finally you need the games and movies that support it.

VR can be traced back to 17th century optics and the invention of the binoculars, too. The idea is simple, the technology required to actually fool your brain has just started to become available in the last few years.
